source: Zhang & Norman (1994) Representations in distributed cognitive tasks
finding: Core theory. A task's representational system is a set of internal and external representations that together represent the abstract task structure. Method: split the task into levels (formal structure, rules, dimensions) and test each level alone.
numbers: Four experiments on Tower of Hanoi (TOH) isomorphs, Cognitive Science 18:87-122.
quote: The basic principle of distributed representations is that the representational system of a distributed cognitive task is a set of internal and external representations.
limits: Theory is descriptive, not a quantitative model. Tested on one task family (TOH) with undergraduates.
agent_relevance: Treat the written form of a problem as part of the task, not a neutral wrapper. Pick the form on purpose (S2/O6).

source: Zhang & Norman (1994) Representations in distributed cognitive tasks
finding: Exp 1A: all rules internal (told in a story, memorised to criterion). Changing the number of rules changed difficulty, but not in a straight line. Fewer rules gives more paths; more rules gives fewer choices.
numbers: N=24 undergraduates, UCSD. Conditions II, II3, II23, II234 (rules 1; 1,3; 1,2,3; 1-4). Minimum solution steps 2, 4, 7, 8. Times, steps and errors divided by minimum steps. Order easiest to hardest by time and errors: II < II3 < II234 ~ II23 (II234 vs II23 not significant). Main effect p<.001 for steps; II vs II23 p<.0001.
limits: Rules were stated in a restaurant story. Different cover story per condition, so story content is a confound the authors did not isolate.
agent_relevance: Problem-space structure alone changes difficulty. A bigger rule set is not automatically harder, so do not assume that more constraints in the prompt always help or hurt.

source: Zhang & Norman (1994) Representations in distributed cognitive tasks
finding: Exp 1B: rule 1 internal, other rules made external (carried by the physical objects). Difficulty still rose with rule number, but participants made no errors at all.
numbers: Order by time: II < II-E3 ~ II-E23 < II-E234. Zero errors in the whole experiment. Main effect p<.0001 for time and for steps.
limits: Exact N not restated in the passage read (same design as 1A). External rules were physical constraints.
agent_relevance: Rules that the medium enforces cost no memory and cause no violations. For an agent, move rules into code or format checks (matches G2, G3).

source: Zhang & Norman (1994) Representations in distributed cognitive tasks
finding: Exp 2 (the key test): same three rules, distributed three ways. All internal (II23, oranges story), two internal and one external (II2-E3, the standard physical TOH), one internal and two external (II-E23). The more rules were external, the easier the problem.
numbers: N=18 undergraduates, within-subject, 6 orders. Main effect p<.05 (time, steps), p<.005 (errors). II23 vs II-E23 errors p<.001. Difficulty: II23 > II2-E3 ~ II-E23 (last pair not significant). All errors were on internal rules; none on external rules.
quote: external rules were either perceptually available or physically constrained
limits: Start and end positions were fixed, not randomised, because of small N. The drop from 2 to 1 internal rule was not significant.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that moving rule-holding out of working memory lowers errors. Strongest base for putting constraints in an external form.

source: Zhang & Norman (1994) Representations in distributed cognitive tasks
finding: Authors' two explanations for the external-rule benefit: (1) external rules are checked by looking, internal ones by mental load that interferes with planning; (2) the recursive strategy (move smallest object first) is easier to find when rules are external.
numbers: From the TOH problem space: once the small or medium disc is home, only 3 more steps are needed. In 54 games by 18 subjects the last 3 steps took 3 steps in 52 games and 5 steps in 2.
limits: Both mechanisms are argued from data, not separated by a dedicated manipulation.
agent_relevance: Two separate gains: cheaper checking and easier strategy discovery. An agent scaffold can target both with an explicit check step and a visible state.

source: Zhang & Norman (1994) Representations in distributed cognitive tasks
finding: Exp 3: nine isomorphs made by crossing the ordinal dimension (size, location, colour) with the nominal dimension (size, location, colour), same three internal rules. Location-coded dimensions beat size and colour.
numbers: Ordinal: location better than size (time p<.01, steps p<.05, errors p<.03). Nominal: location better than size and colour (time p<.003, errors p<.0001). Size vs colour not significant. No significant interactions.
limits: Authors cannot say why location wins; they link it to Treisman and Gelade (1980) and Nissen (1985): location is needed to bind separate colour and size maps. Colour order (red>green>yellow) was easy to memorise, so internal ordinal coding cost little.
agent_relevance: Spatial position is a cheap, reliable way to carry order and identity. For a text agent, layout (rows, columns, grid) may stand in for location.

source: Zhang & Norman (1994) Representations in distributed cognitive tasks
finding: Authors claim: same formal structure, different isomorphic representations activate different processes; confusing a distributed representation with an internal one leads to over-complex accounts of cognition.
numbers: Statement in General Discussion; no extra numbers.
limits: Claim rests on TOH only; Zhang 1997 extended it to other tasks.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a model uses the same process on two isomorphic phrasings. Test phrasings, do not trust equivalence.

source: Kotovsky, Hayes & Simon (1985) Why are some problems hard? Evidence from Tower of Hanoi
finding: Earlier TOH isomorph studies (Dish-move vs Peg-move) showed isomorphs differ strongly in difficulty. Zhang and Norman's Exp 2 matches their time ordering (as reported in Zhang & Norman's discussion).
numbers: Zhang & Norman say their steps and errors agree with Kotovsky et al.'s solution times; no figures taken from the 1985 paper.
limits: Known only through Zhang & Norman's discussion and memory; not opened.
agent_relevance: Same logical problem can differ in difficulty by form; prior art for any isomorph-based test.

source: Larkin & Simon (1987) Why a diagram is (sometimes) worth ten thousand words
finding: Computational model. Two representations can hold equal information yet not be computationally equivalent. Diagrams index information by location, so related items sit together; this cuts search and aids recognition. Production-system models were run on a pulley problem and a supply-and-demand problem.
numbers: No numbers recorded; wiley page blocked (HTTP 403), so not read this session.
limits: Not opened. The title word 'sometimes' marks the limit: a diagram helps only if the needed inferences are easy to recognise.
agent_relevance: Gives the formal test for O6: pick the form that makes the next inference a cheap lookup, not the one with the most information.

source: Gigerenzer & Hoffrage (1995) How to improve Bayesian reasoning without instruction: frequency formats
finding: Natural-frequency formats raise correct Bayesian answers compared with probability formats. This is the standard 'format helps reasoning' result behind the card/token Bayesian tasks.
numbers: From memory only: roughly 16% correct with probabilities vs about 46% with natural frequencies. Not verified this session.
limits: Not opened. Numbers unverified; check before use. Later work disputes whether format or nested-set structure is the cause.
agent_relevance: For a probability task, restate in counts of cases (natural frequencies) before reasoning; cheap and testable.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Mind's Eye of LLMs: Visualization-of-Thought elicits spatial reasoning (NeurIPS)
finding: Visualization-of-Thought (VoT): the model draws a text grid of the state after each reasoning step. On three spatial tasks GPT-4 VoT beat GPT-4 CoT and GPT-4 with visualisation disabled.
numbers: Table parsed from PDF text; row order inferred. Visual tiling: VoT 63.94 vs CoT 54.15 vs no-viz 46.98 vs GPT-4V CoT 49.62. Route planning completing rate: 40.77 vs 37.02 vs 37.17 vs 33.36; success rate 14.72 vs 9.48 vs 10.28 vs 5.65. Natural-language navigation: 59.00 vs 54.00 vs 35.50 (VoT beats no-viz by 23.5 points). p<.05 by z-test except VoT vs CoT on NL navigation (p<.16).
limits: Table layout garbled in extraction; mapping cross-checked only against the text's 23.5-point claim. Route-planning success stays low (14.7%).
agent_relevance: Writing the state as a grid after each step is a cheap external form that helped a text-only model. Candidate for O6.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Visualization-of-Thought
finding: VoT's drawn states are often wrong, but when right the model decides well. Drawing accuracy is the bottleneck.
numbers: Final-visualisation check: compliance with constraints 51.14% (navigation) and 52.01% (tiling); state accuracy 26.48% and 24.25%; correct decisions given an accurate drawing 65.16% and 77.20%.
limits: Measured only in the VoT condition with GPT-4; no human baseline in the passage read.
agent_relevance: Gain comes from accurate state tracking. A code check of the drawn state (G2, G3) should add more than drawing alone.

source: Wu et al. (2024) Visualization-of-Thought
finding: Boundary condition: when a task can be turned into arithmetic, drawing does not help. In ring navigation GPT-4 normalised moves to (15-3) mod 12.
numbers: 200 test instances, ring size 12: CoT 52.5% vs VoT 49.5%. Smaller models (GPT-3.5, LLaMA3-8B) gained little and guessed at random on route planning; LLaMA3-70B VoT beat baseline on all tasks except visual tiling.
limits: Small difference on 200 items; no significance test reported in the passage read.
agent_relevance: Choose the form to match the task: calculation form for modular arithmetic, grid form for spatial tracking. Do not apply a visual form blindly.

source: Menon, Zemel & Vondrick (2024) Whiteboard-of-Thought: thinking step-by-step across modalities
finding: The model writes code that draws a figure, then reads the rendered image. It beat chain-of-thought on four visual/spatial tasks given as text (ASCII art, spatial navigation).
numbers: Abstract: settings where GPT-4o CoT scores 0% and whiteboard-of-thought reaches up to 92%. Hexagon-grid navigation: 8% CoT to 61% WoT. On square grids WoT is lower than CoT, because CoT can use 2D-grid knowledge from text.
limits: Needs a multimodal model that can read the render. Gains are task-specific; errors come from wrong code and wrong image reading.
agent_relevance: A rendered picture is a stronger external form for some problems than a typed one. Tests whether code-made diagrams beat text-made ones.

source: Wang et al. (2024) Is a picture worth a thousand words? Delving into spatial reasoning for vision language models (SpatialEval)
finding: Counter-example to 'a diagram always helps'. Adding an image often hurt vision-language models on spatial tasks, compared with the text description.
numbers: Most VLMs scored below their same-backbone LLM on Spatial-Map and Spatial-Grid (e.g. Mixtral-7B 62.1% on Spatial-Grid). Removing the image raised LLaVA-1.6-34B by 20.1% on Spatial-Grid. Text-only Llama-3 reached 71.9% and Mistral-7B 62.1% on Spatial-Grid.
limits: 2024 open VLMs; stronger closed models may differ. Several models were near or below random on Spatial-Map and Maze-Nav.
agent_relevance: The Larkin-Simon diagram advantage does not transfer automatically: it depends on whether the model can read the form. Test each form per model.

source: Wang et al. (2024) SpatialEval
finding: VLMs largely ignore the image: replacing the matching image by Gaussian noise or a random image still improved accuracy over the original image.
numbers: Reported as gains across VLM architectures in Figures 9 and 10; per-model figures not extracted.
limits: Shows VLMs lean on the text and treat the image as noise; not a claim that images are useless for all models.
agent_relevance: The same facts in two forms can be redundant; the model uses the form it reads best. Do not add forms hoping for extra signal.

source: Sui et al. (2024) Table Meets LLM: can LLMs understand structured table data? (SUC benchmark)
finding: Serialisation format changes accuracy on table tasks. HTML was best on most of seven tasks; natural-language-plus-separator was weaker on several.
numbers: GPT-4 size detection: HTML 83.43%, XML 80.21%, Markdown 82.12%, NL+Sep 73.12%. GPT-4 column retrieval: HTML 69.32, XML 68.28, JSON 64.32, NL+Sep 66.32, Markdown 60.12. GPT-3.5 size detection HTML 67.00% vs NL+Sep 42.00%. GPT-4 tested on 300 samples per task.
limits: No format wins everywhere: GPT-3.5 reverse lookup was best for XML (55.00) and worst for HTML (47.33). Many gaps are 1-3 points on 300 items.
agent_relevance: Table form matters but is task-dependent. Pick per task; for structure questions HTML-like tags helped.

source: Sui et al. (2024) Table Meets LLM
finding: Best combination: HTML markup plus format explanation, role prompt, and keeping the original order. Format cues help when stacked.
numbers: Best combo averaged 65.43% over seven tasks. Ablation (GPT-3.5 HTML): moving the question before the table lowered size detection by 14.33 points and merged-cell detection by 11.00; removing partition marks cost 2-4 points on several tasks.
limits: Ablation deltas from a single run per cell; no variance given.
agent_relevance: Where the question sits relative to the data is part of the representation. Test question-after-data.

source: He et al. (2024) Does prompt formatting have any impact on LLM performance?
finding: Plain text, Markdown, YAML and JSON prompts gave significantly different scores for GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 families; newer/larger models were more robust.
numbers: Best vs worst format differed at p<.01 for most model-benchmark pairs (one-sided matched-pair t-tests). FIND: 200% gain going Markdown to plain text (GPT-3.5). HumanEval: over 300% gain JSON to plain text (GPT-4-32k-0613). MMLU: GPT-3.5 gave only 16% identical answers between Markdown and JSON; GPT-4 consistency above 0.5.
limits: No single best format across models; gains quoted as relative percentages from low bases. OpenAI models only.
agent_relevance: Format is a real source of variance. Choose forms by measuring on our task, and report spread across forms.

source: Sclar et al. (2024) Quantifying language models' sensitivity to spurious features in prompt design
finding: Meaning-preserving format changes (separators, casing, spacing) swing few-shot accuracy by up to 76 points on LLaMA-2-13B. Sensitivity persisted with larger models, more shots and instruction tuning.
numbers: Up to 76 accuracy points on LLaMA-2-13B (abstract); per-task tables not extracted.
limits: Open-source 2023 models, few-shot. Superficial formatting, not structural re-representation of the kind Zhang and Norman study.
agent_relevance: Measure the spread of any scaffold over trivial format variants before crediting a gain (relates to G4).

source: Fatemi, Halcrow & Perozzi (2023) Talk like a graph: encoding graphs for large language models
finding: How a graph is written as text changes accuracy, depending on encoder, task and graph structure. Encoder choice gave 4.8% to 61.8% gain.
numbers: Connected-nodes task: adjacency encoding 19.8% vs incident encoding 53.8%. Incident beat the rest on node degree and connected nodes. Zero-shot CoT was worse than plain zero-shot on basic graph tasks.
limits: Synthetic graphs, PaLM-class models; no human comparison.
agent_relevance: Larkin-Simon logic reappears: the form that puts related facts next to each other (incident lists) wins. Rewrite relations so neighbours are adjacent.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Visual Sketchpad: sketching as a visual chain of thought for multimodal language models
finding: Giving multimodal models a drawing tool (lines, boxes, marks, auxiliary geometry) improved math and vision tasks over the same models without sketching.
numbers: Average gain 12.7% on math tasks and 8.6% on vision tasks (abstract); Table 1 text: 11.2% for GPT-4o and 23.4% for GPT-4 Turbo. Max-flow: GPT-4o 66.3%, +41.3 over base. Convexity and parity: GPT-4 Turbo above 90%. Game strategy gains 3-10%. V*Bench 80.3%, BLINK spatial 83.9%.
limits: Needs multimodal models and tools; vision-specialist modules sometimes fail. Gain differs by model (relative depth: GPT-4o +12.1, GPT-4 Turbo +2.4).
agent_relevance: Self-made diagrams (not given ones) help. Supports an operator where the agent builds its own diagram before solving.

source: Liu et al. (2022) Mind's Eye: grounded language model reasoning through simulation
finding: Running a physics engine (MuJoCo) and pasting its result into the prompt grounded LM answers on physical reasoning. A small model with the simulation matched a model 100x larger.
numbers: Average gain 27.9% zero-shot and 46.0% few-shot over 39 tasks. GPT-3 1.3B + Mind's Eye 29.8% vs GPT-3 175B vanilla 29% zero-shot. One task: 36.4 to 38.2 with vanilla LM vs 46.7 to 84.2 with simulation; another 68.6 to 99.1.
limits: Narrow physics-alignment benchmark; needs a text-to-simulator converter, whose errors cost a few points.
agent_relevance: An externally computed state beats model-internal guessing. Fits the schema rule: code produces the representation, model reads it.

source: Zhang (1997) The nature of external representations in problem solving
finding: Follow-up to the 1994 work: external representations are not just memory aids. They give perceptual cues, constrain action and change the task (tic-tac-toe isomorphs, number scrabble), from memory.
numbers: No numbers taken; not opened.
limits: Not opened; description from memory.
agent_relevance: Same idea beyond TOH; supports the claim that form alters the task itself.

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action
finding: In Tetris, players rotate pieces to learn the fit, not just to place them. Acting on the external form can be cheaper than mental computation.
numbers: No numbers recorded; not opened. Overlaps sibling subfield 07_epistemic_actions.
limits: Not opened; cross-link only.
agent_relevance: The agent may act on the external form (reorder, annotate) to compute. Covered in the epistemic-actions subfield.
